analysis.investment_thesis: Eris Lifesciences trades at INR 1,446 against a Graham Number of ~INR 369 (P/E 45x, P/B 6.4x) — a 75% premium to intrinsic value with zero margin of safety. Worse, a debt explosion from zero to INR 2,478 Cr in three years has caused finance costs (INR 231 Cr in FY25) to consume 62% of net profit, leaving earnings flat despite a near-doubling of revenue.
key_strengths: Nine consecutive years of positive net profit (2016–2025) — a genuine earnings record
Strong operating margin of 26.4% and gross margin of 73.9% reflect durable branded pharma pricing
OCF positive all 5 years with FY25 operating cash flow surging to INR 1,065 Cr
key_risks: Debt explosion: borrowings went from INR 0 (FY20) to INR 2,389 Cr (FY25); D/E now 0.68 vs Graham's 0.5 limit
Finance costs grew from INR 4 Cr (FY22) to INR 231 Cr (FY25), suppressing net profit which is actually down from FY22's INR 406 Cr to FY25's INR 375 Cr
Acquisition binge (Investing CF -INR 1,828 Cr in FY24 alone) introduces integration risk and inflated goodwill on the balance sheet
red_flags: Graham Number ~INR 369 vs market price INR 1,446 — stock is priced at 4x intrinsic value by my formula
P/E of 45.2 is 3x my upper limit of 15; P/B of 6.37 is over 4x my preferred ceiling of 1.5
Net profit DECLINED from INR 406 Cr (FY22) to INR 375 Cr (FY25) while revenue nearly doubled — the earnings 'E' is being hollowed out by debt servicing
Finance costs of INR 231 Cr represent 38% of EBIT — interest coverage is dangerously thin for a company Mr. Market prices as a compounder
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Eris Lifesciences fails every quantitative test I have developed over decades of security analysis. The P/E of 45.2 is nearly three times my absolute ceiling. The P/B of 6.37 means you are paying INR 6.37 for every rupee of net assets — the market is pricing in a great deal of future speculation, not present reality. My Graham Number, calculated as √(22.5 × EPS₂₅ × BVPS₂₅) = √(22.5 × 27.1 × 223), yields roughly INR 369. The current price of INR 1,446 represents a 292% premium to that figure. I require a discount to intrinsic value, not a four-fold premium.

The balance sheet deterioration is what troubles me most. This company had virtually no debt in FY20; by FY25 it carries INR 2,478 Cr of debt with finance costs of INR 231 Cr — almost two-thirds of net profit. Revenue has grown impressively at 19.2% CAGR, and EBITDA has followed, but the net profit available to common shareholders has gone nowhere: INR 406 Cr in FY22, INR 374 Cr in FY23, INR 397 Cr in FY24, INR 375 Cr in FY25. This is the illusion of growth — reported at the top line, confiscated at the bottom by bankers. The intelligent investor does not pay 45 times earnings for a business whose true owner earnings are stagnant and whose debt load is rising sharply. Until this stock trades at or below its Graham Number — which would require a price decline exceeding 70% — I have no interest.
